Case finding

Working identification: two recurring acoustic families are labeled Bird A and Bird B, conditional on the supplied field observation that two birds were calling. These are local source hypotheses, not independently verified identities. The strongest demonstration pair is C01 at 1.35-1.96 s, labeled an alarm candidate, followed by C02 at 2.49-2.89 s, labeled a response candidate.

Evidence levelFinding
Measured in this fileRepeated contrasting harmonic contours, approximate event timing, a selected short-note train, and nearly duplicated audio channels.
Provided field contextTwo birds; alert/alarm activity with intervening clucks. This context is preserved, not claimed as independently discovered.
Interpretation to testA and B exchange calls; the later call is contingent on the earlier one rather than a shared disturbance.
Not establishedPhysical individual, sex, breed, exact predator class, acknowledgment meaning, word translation, or syntax.

Central conclusion: this is a useful, testable interaction case - not merely a list of chicken sounds. It supports asking how one animal's signal changes another animal's next action. It does not, by itself, prove conversational intent or language.

2 | Repeated timing and the short clucks

A second A?-to-B candidate occurs at 9.27-10.74 s. The lower confidence in C05's source makes this corroborating pattern weaker than an independently confirmed second exchange. Prominent bouts form A - B - A - A? - A? - B - A - A?, not a perfectly alternating dialogue.

Selected energy peaks occur at 6.864 s, 7.131 s, 7.379 s, 7.645 s, 7.872 s, 8.136 s, 8.405 s, 8.645 s, and 8.925 s. The mean interval is 0.258 s (about 3.88 selected notes/s); the median is 0.265 s. These are local descriptive measures, not a flock-wide calling rate. The selected energy cores are roughly 0.04-0.08 s long under the stated threshold method.

Their repeated occurrence is not equivalent to conversational punctuation. Possible functions include maintaining contact, continuing vigilance, or expressing a state of arousal. Those are alternative hypotheses, not translations. In particular, "acknowledgment" and "all clear" remain untested. A short note's source cannot be assigned to B simply because it follows A.

3 | Separating voice, call type, and context

Acoustic family A

The clearest A examples are C01, C03, and C07. They have comparatively extended, dipping-then-sustained harmonic structure. A prominent low ridge lies around 0.9-1.1 kHz, with energy in several higher bands. A ridge is not necessarily the fundamental frequency: doubled components, subharmonics, or overlapping sound can produce misleading pitch estimates.

Acoustic family B

C02 and C06 share a lower rising harmonic ladder, with a visible low component approximately 0.45-0.60 kHz and a conspicuous band around 1 kHz. Their selected durations are about 0.40 and 0.45 s, compared with roughly 0.60-0.64 s for the A/A? windows. Repeated contour differences justify keeping two acoustic families separate; they do not by themselves prove two anatomical callers.

Why several A labels have a question mark

C04, C05, and C08 have more complex mixtures of partials. They are compatible with the broad A-family pattern, but a change in call production or an overlapping source could produce similar complexity. The annotations therefore retain A? rather than silently promoting them to verified Bird A calls. There was no source separation or validated individual-identity model in this analysis.

The decoded file has two 48 kHz channels, but their correlation is 0.99993. The channel-difference RMS is about 38.5 dB below the mono-average RMS. They are effectively duplicated mono for this purpose. Stereo channel position cannot identify the two birds, and recording level alone cannot establish distance, sex, dominance, or urgency. The video is a spectrogram display, not camera footage.

4 | What the chicken literature establishes

Calls can provide information about external events

Evans, Evans and Marler (1993) investigated the functional reference of chicken alarm calls: playback-based receiver behavior supports a distinction between calls associated with aerial and terrestrial danger. This is important because the receiver need not see the original triggering event for the signal to guide its behavior. The experimental function of a call is not equivalent to a human word or a demonstrated conscious proposition. [1]

Evans and Evans (1999) found that hens hearing food calls performed a specific downward-looking, feeding-related response absent in the comparison conditions. Food calls and ground alarms were described as acoustically similar, yet their behavioral effects differed. This is a direct reason not to classify a short cluck solely by how it sounds to a human observer. [2]

The audience can change whether a chicken calls

Karakashian, Gyger and Marler (1988) found that male aerial alarm calling was increased by conspecific audiences. Their manipulations included companions of different ages and relationships and controls for cues from the audience. Social modulation makes a purely mechanical "sound comes out whenever fear rises" description inadequate, without requiring a claim of human-like intention or theory of mind. [3]

Alarm signals can vary by degree as well as kind

Wilson and Evans (2012) reported that alarm structure varied with the size, speed and proximity of avian stimuli. Closer, larger or faster stimuli elicited shorter, louder, clearer, lower-frequency alarms; their playback experiment supported a receiver effect of call amplitude. Thus categorical function and graded acoustic variation can coexist. This does not license reading urgency directly from an uncalibrated recording. [4]

Reception can extend beyond the chicken flock

Zhang and colleagues (2023) played wild Japanese tit calls to free-range domestic chickens. The chickens were more vigilant to alarm calls than to territorial song and differed in their responses to the alarm treatments. This makes ecological information exchange a plausible wider research topic for a mixed-species soundscape. It does not identify another species in Chicken_032. [5]

What transfers to this recording: chicken signals can be informative and socially consequential, so a real exchange is a serious biological hypothesis. What does not transfer automatically: the exact call labels, individual identities, trigger category, or response meaning in this particular 15-second recording.

5 | In what sense is this language-like?

Best formulation: a possible example of reciprocal signaling with some functional ingredients also needed for language. "Primitive precursor" is useful only as a loose analogy. Chickens are not a stage through which human language is now passing, and this recording cannot establish the historical evolutionary origin of speech.

First ingredient: information beyond the sound itself

When a receiver changes its behavior appropriately after hearing a call, the signal can give it information about an event it did not directly witness. Chicken alarm and food-call playback findings motivate this possibility. Information transfer is more specific than simply noticing that two animals make noises. Nevertheless, externally referential behavior does not, alone, specify whether the bird represents a noun, a command, an emotional state, or a learned predictive association. [1,2]

Second ingredient: sensitivity to a recipient

Audience effects show that call production is embedded in a social situation. A language-like comparison concerns the relation among a signal, a sender, and a receiver, rather than vocabulary alone. A listener-sensitive system need not possess human perspective-taking. [3]

Third ingredient: contingent timing and feedback

The specific possibility in this clip is a loop: A signals, B changes state or calls, and A's next behavior may depend on B. The two A-B-A-like passages make that hypothesis worth testing. They do not yet distinguish it from both birds reacting to one continuing disturbance. "Response" describes a proposed relation between events, not a unique waveform category.

In another bird species, Benichov and Vallentin (2020) experimentally linked a premotor inhibitory circuit to zebra finches' response timing and avoidance of vocal overlap. This demonstrates that turn timing can be actively controlled in a bird. It is a comparator, not evidence that the same mechanism or behavioral result has been demonstrated in these chickens. [6]

A much higher bar: combinations whose meaning depends on order

Suzuki, Wheatcroft and Griesser (2016) tested Japanese tits with separated and combined call elements. Danger-scanning and approach responses combined in the natural sequence and were reduced when the sequence was reversed. That is a stronger kind of evidence for composition than simply detecting repeated note order. No equivalent manipulation or receiver measurement exists in Chicken_032. [7]

Interpretive ceiling: candidate information exchange and temporal coordination. Not established here: stable word meanings, acknowledgment semantics, compositional syntax, deliberate teaching, displacement, or open-ended generative language. The absence of proof in this clip is not proof that the birds lack every relevant capacity.

6 | Turning this case into a research program

Start by observing who does what

The highest-value next data are synchronized bird-visible video and longer uncut audio before and after natural episodes. Maintain stable individual IDs when they can be verified without disturbing the birds. Log who vocalizes, who looks up or scans sideways, who freezes, who approaches, and who resumes feeding. Record potential triggers and whether each animal could see them. A truly separated, synchronized microphone array can strengthen source attribution; two copies of one audio channel cannot.

Test interaction rather than selected coincidences

Predefine response windows and annotate all eligible A calls and B calls, including nonresponses. Compare the probability of B calling after A with B's probability during matched no-A periods. Also ask whether A changes subsequent calling after B. Account for the birds' recent call history, ongoing alarm state, movement and shared external events. The present two selected A-to-B links are insufficient for a reliable significance test.

A useful null analysis shifts one verified caller's event train relative to the other within comparable sessions, preserving each bird's local calling structure while disrupting precise alignment. Carefully choose shifts and matched windows so the null does not mix quiet and alarm states. Use independent sessions and birds for replication. A timestamp relation alone is not a causal demonstration.

Make the competing hypotheses produce different predictions

Recipient response: B's call probability depends on A after contextual controls. Shared trigger: both depend principally on the same disturbance. Contact function for clucks: clucks predict orientation or approach. Safety-related function: specific clucks predict relaxed behavior beyond what is expected as the disturbance fades. These predictions should be scored from independent behavior, not inferred from the sound label being tested.

Playback is a later, controlled step

A carefully designed playback study could compare a candidate alarm, a candidate short note, their natural ordering, a reversed ordering and appropriate control sounds. But unfamiliar or repeated alarm playbacks can create a welfare confound. Begin with passive observation; any experiment should be reviewed with an avian behavior or welfare specialist, use suitable exposure limits and stopping rules, and avoid deliberately exposing birds to predators. The planned test must measure recipient behavior, not just whether it vocalizes.

The strongest research question is bidirectional: not only "Does B answer A?" but "Does B's answer alter what A does next?" That would move the analysis from temporal succession toward a closed interaction loop.

7 | Annotation contract and reproducibility

Keep four layers separate in ChickenNet

Acoustics: falling harmonic bout, rising harmonic ladder, short cluck-like note. Source: A, B, A? or U, with verification status. Function: alarm, alert, contact or unassigned, with the evidence for each. Interaction: initiator candidate, response candidate, possible return, with the event it may respond to. Confidence should be recorded separately for these layers.

The data package uses proposed labels rather than gold labels. A response candidate can itself be an alarm; the two terms are not alternatives. A proposed response requires temporal context, so it should not become a stand-alone "response sound" class trained from cropped waveforms alone. Keep ambiguous and overlapping intervals instead of forcing every sound into A or B.

Analysis settings

ItemSetting
AudioAAC source decoded to float PCM; 48,000 Hz; analyzed samples 0-719,999; mean of two near-identical channels.
Main spectrumHann window 2,048 samples (42.67 ms); hop 256 samples (5.33 ms); bin spacing 23.44 Hz.
Harmonic detailHann window 4,096 samples (85.33 ms); hop 256 samples.
Short notesHann window 1,024 samples; hop 128 samples. Local maxima in nine manually chosen windows; 18% local peak energy defines approximate cores.
Spectral features500-5,500 Hz excess power after a per-frequency 20th-percentile background estimate. Values describe the mixed recording, not isolated callers or fundamental frequency.
Review mediaAnnotated 1,920 x 1,080 MP4; 10 frames/s; 15 seconds. Original AAC stream copied without filtering or gain changes.

Short-window spectra emphasize timing but blur nearby harmonics; longer windows clarify harmonics but smear fast boundaries. Numerical bin spacing is not a guarantee of practical resolution or boundary accuracy. No independent source localization, semantic decoder or validated identity classifier was used.

A concrete cropping issue: the second alarm candidate at 9.27-9.87 s and its response candidate at 10.29-10.74 s fall on opposite sides of a 10-second cut. Non-overlapping 5-second clips would separate them. Retain the original sequence and event links. Split train, validation and test by source recording and session - and by bird when appropriate - before cropping. Keep human presence annotations separate from these interaction proposals.
